gbs333-h59932-d1e102.summary: States the single question of Distinction 25: whether the faithful of both testaments are bound to believe explicitly all the articles of faith sufficiently and specifically distinguished in the Apostles' Creed.

gbs333-h59932-d1e120.summary: Announces the three-article structure: declarations of terms, conclusions, and solutions of doubts.

gbs333-h59932-d1e133.summary: First notandum, on the Creed. Although everything to be believed is in canonical Scripture, Scripture is vast, so before dispersing, the apostles gathered certain principal truths, to which the rest can be reduced, for easier understanding and memory. This collection is called the symbolum, from syn ('together') and bolos ('morsel'), since each apostle contributed his piece. Its articles are distinguished by content or by author. By content there are fourteen: seven concern God in his own nature, seven the assumed nature. Of the first seven, four concern God intrinsically: the unity of nature ('I believe in God', one, not many) and the three persons (Father almighty; Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord; the Holy Spirit). The preposition 'in' is placed only before these, because we believe 'in' God alone as first truth and highest good to be loved above all, which is to cling to God by believing love (d. 23), every creature being subject to vanity (Romans 8).
claims: The apostles composed the Creed as a compendium of principal truths to which all others can be reduced.
By content the Creed has fourteen articles: seven on the divinity, seven on the humanity.
'Credo in' is used only for the divine nature and persons, since only God is believed in as first truth and highest good.

gbs333-h59932-d1e260.summary: The other three divinity articles express the three operations proper to God with respect to their effects in creatures: creating (producing from nothing), justifying (forgiving sins), and beatifying (conferring eternal life), which belong to God alone.
claims: Creating, justifying, and beatifying belong to God alone.

gbs333-h59932-d1e280.summary: These operations terminate in three participated beings in the creature: nature by creation, grace by justification, and glory by beatification (Ps.: 'the Lord will give grace and glory'). 'Creator of heaven and earth' expresses creation. 'Holy Catholic Church, communion of saints, forgiveness of sins' together express justification. In justifying the wicked, the infusion of grace and charity forgives sins, makes the sinner pleasing to God, and incorporates him into the Church as a living member in merit, not only in number, and there is no forgiveness outside the Church. The communion of saints follows, by which the justified share in all the goods of all the saints ('I am a partaker of all who fear you'), since charity makes all things common. So these three form one article.
claims: Creation, justification, and beatification confer the being of nature, grace, and glory.
Church, communion of saints, and forgiveness of sins together form one article on justification.
There is no forgiveness of sins outside the Church.
Through charity the justified share in the goods of all the saints.

gbs333-h59932-d1e352.summary: The third operation, beatification, is expressed in 'resurrection of the flesh and eternal life', since perfect beatitude includes the glory of body and soul conferred after the resurrection. This completes the seven articles about God in himself, intrinsically and in his proper extrinsic operations.
claims: Perfect beatitude includes the glory of both body and soul after resurrection.

gbs333-h59932-d1e376.summary: Lists the seven articles concerning Christ in his assumed nature: conception (the incarnation of the Word), birth from an incorrupt virgin, the passion (comprising crucifixion, death, and burial as one article), descent into hell, resurrection, ascension, and coming to judgment, since he will judge in human form.
claims: The seven humanity articles are conception, virgin birth, passion, descent into hell, resurrection, ascension, and coming to judgment.

gbs333-h59932-d1e405.summary: For the first seven articles the apostles did not keep the order just given but followed two orders suited to the understanding and memory of the simple. First, the order of nature and persons: nature is prior, as one in all three persons, so the unity article comes first. Among the persons, the order of origin governs. Since the first person is the Father, to whom power is appropriated, the unity article is followed by two Father articles: one on his proper ('Father') and one on his appropriated ('almighty, creator of heaven and earth', since creation pertains to omnipotence).
claims: The Creed orders its articles for the ease of understanding and memory of the simple.
The unity of nature comes first, then the persons in order of origin.
Power and creation are appropriated to the Father.

gbs333-h59932-d1e455.summary: Next come all the articles about the Son: first his divine nature, then those of the assumed humanity, ending with the coming to judgment in human form (Acts 1). Then the Holy Spirit, third person, followed by the two operations of the Trinity appropriated to the Spirit, the justification and glorification of the wicked, whose principle is divine goodness, appropriated to the Spirit. He is ruler and sanctifier of the Church, the communion of saints as uncreated charity communicating each one's goods to all, the forgiveness of sins, and the one who illuminates and kindles to vision and fruition. This order suits understanding. For memory they also partly kept the order of time: creation, the first temporal work, after the eternal articles; then the incarnation and the deeds and sufferings in the flesh in temporal order; then the Spirit with his works ending in final retribution.
claims: Justification and glorification are appropriated to the Holy Spirit as divine goodness.
The Holy Spirit as uncreated charity is the communion of saints.
The Creed also follows temporal order to aid memory.

gbs333-h59932-d1e539.summary: Distinguishing the articles by authors gives twelve, one for each apostle, though this division is confused, since some apostles contributed several articles and others parts. Aquinas and Scotus agree that Peter, head of the apostles, combined the first three (unity, the Father's omnipotence, creation), concerning the Father as source of the Trinity. John contributed the Son, James the Greater the conception and birth, Andrew the passion, Philip the descent, Thomas the resurrection, Bartholomew the ascension, Matthew the coming to judgment, James son of Alphaeus the Holy Spirit, Simon the Church and communion of saints, Jude the forgiveness of sins, and Matthias (or Thomas) glory. Bonaventure and others assign them differently, but it matters little, since the one Holy Spirit revealed the faith to the apostles and is the Creed's principal author.
claims: The Creed can be divided into twelve articles by apostolic author.
The assignment of articles to apostles is disputed and of little importance.
The Holy Spirit is the principal author of the Creed.
concepts: Peter as head of the apostles

gbs333-h59932-d1e628.summary: Two further creeds were added to the Apostles' Creed for fuller explanation of the faith and refutation of heresies: the Nicene and the Athanasian. The Athanasian Creed was composed against Arius and so stresses the unity of the divine essence, the distinction of persons, and Christ's equality with the Father in divinity and inferiority in humanity.
claims: The Nicene and Athanasian creeds explain the faith and refute heresies.
The Athanasian Creed was directed against Arianism.

gbs333-h59932-d1e652.summary: Following Bonaventure, the Nicene Creed refutes many heresies. Against the Manichaeans' two principles it says 'one God, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible'. Against Arius it says 'one Lord Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son... through whom all things were made'. Against those who made the Spirit a servant it says 'Lord and giver of life'. Against the Greeks it says 'who proceeds from the Father and the Son'. Against those who called the prophets frenzied it says 'who spoke through the prophets'. It omits the descent into hell, since few erred about it. The Apostles' Creed is said secretly at Prime and Compline, since it was composed before the faith was published, while the other two, composed after, are said publicly on certain days, the Nicene at Mass and the Athanasian at Prime.
claims: Each Nicene clause targets a specific heresy (Manichaean, Arian, pneumatomachian, Greek, anti-prophetic).
The Apostles' Creed is recited secretly because it was composed before the faith was published.

gbs333-h59932-d1e726.summary: Second notandum: faith is explicit or implicit. Explicit faith is actual assent to a Catholic truth, universal or particular, such as 'everything revealed by God is true', 'the biblical canon is true', or 'Christ fed five thousand'. Implicit faith is habitual or actual assent to a general proposition including many particular truths, namely all that can be inferred from it by good consequence, immediately or with a true added premise. Assent to 'everything in canonical Scripture is true' is implicit faith in every particular truth in the canon (creation, Adam's expulsion, the Last Supper).
claims: Explicit faith is actual assent to a particular or universal Catholic truth.
Implicit faith is assent to a general proposition from which particular truths follow.

gbs333-h59932-d1e789.summary: First corollary: all habitual faith is implicit faith in the truths to whose assent it inclines.
claims: Habitual faith is implicit faith in what it inclines to.

gbs333-h59932-d1e796.summary: Second corollary: the same actual faith is explicit and implicit regarding different things. Assenting to 'whatever the Church believes is Catholic truth' is explicit faith in that proposition and implicit faith in all truths the Church believes and all that follows from it with a true added premise, e.g. 'the Gospel contains Catholic truth', since the Church believes the Gospel.
claims: One act of faith can be explicit regarding one proposition and implicit regarding its consequences.
Belief that whatever the Church believes is true is implicit faith in all the Church believes.

gbs333-h59932-d1e843.summary: Third corollary: whoever has infused faith implicitly believes all credibles, even without actually apprehending anything. So baptized infants without the use of reason implicitly believe everything to be believed.
claims: Infused faith is implicit belief in all credibles.
Baptized infants implicitly believe all that is to be believed.

gbs333-h59932-d1e856.summary: Fourth corollary: one can implicitly believe a truth while explicitly dissenting from it and even assenting to its opposite. Someone who believes whatever the Church believes is true, but thinks the Church holds that Abraham had only one wife, implicitly believes he had two and explicitly disbelieves it. This implicit faith is most useful, for, as Ockham (De sacramento altaris c. 1) and Gerson say, it protects from all heresy: one who believes whatever the Church believes never adheres pertinaciously to error and corrects it once shown the Church's belief. Ockham's Dialogus: to believe implicitly is to assent firmly to a universal from which much follows and to adhere pertinaciously to nothing contrary, and such a person is Catholic. Innocent III and the gloss on c. Damnamus add that one who, moved by natural reason, wrongly thinks the Father greater than the Son or the persons spatially apart, but not pertinaciously and subjecting his opinion to the Church, is neither heretic nor sinner. Indeed, if the error is invincible, implicit faith preserves merit: a simple person who, after due inquiry, believes his prelate's erroneous preaching for God's sake, thinking it the Church's belief, merits by believing a falsehood from charity, since only acting against culpably erroneous conscience is sinful.
claims: One can implicitly believe what one explicitly disbelieves.
Implicit faith in whatever the Church believes protects against heresy, because it excludes pertinacity.
Non-pertinacious error, subordinated to the Church's faith, is neither heresy nor sin.
A simple believer who invincibly errs by following a prelate's erroneous preaching can merit, acting from charity.
Only acting against a culpably erroneous conscience is sinful; invincible error is not culpable.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1041.summary: Third notandum: the faithful are of two kinds. The greater (maiores) have the office of governing and teaching by word of truth and example of virtue, such as pastors, bishops, curates, and university lecturers, especially in theology. The lesser (minores) are the simple and subjects who need teaching and governance. Augustine (De Trin. XIV.1) distinguishes knowing what one must know for eternal life from knowing how to help the pious and defend against the impious, and many have faith without this knowledge. So the greater must believe, defend the faith, and instruct the simple, and the lesser are instructed, nourished, and strengthened by them. This ends article 1.
claims: The faithful divide into the greater, who teach and govern, and the lesser, who are taught.
The greater must not only believe but defend the faith and instruct the simple.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1119.summary: Article 2, first conclusion: infused faith was necessary for all to be saved in every state of the Church, and the act of faith was necessary for adults using reason. First part: the soul is not accepted by God unless perfected by a supernatural habit in the intellect as in the will (charity), and since understanding naturally precedes willing, the intellect is perfected first (in nature, not time). So faith, like charity, was necessary in every state after the fall, even before Christ. The two can be separated in this life (unformed faith in one in mortal sin), but by his ordained law God perfects the whole soul (Deut. 32; John 7) and does not perfect the will by charity without perfecting the intellect by faith. Authorities: Habakkuk 2, Romans 1, Galatians 3, Hebrews 11. Second part: those without the use of reason are saved by the Redeemer's merit alone, but for those with reason one's own merit is required ('keep the commandments'; 'faith without works is dead'). Merit requires actual faith directing the intention to the end, as actual prudence directs virtuous acts. Faith is the charioteer of meritorious acts, so the act of faith is necessary for those using reason with the same necessity as meritorious acts.
claims: Infused faith was necessary for salvation in every state of the Church, including before Christ.
God's ordained law does not perfect the will by charity without perfecting the intellect by faith.
Those without reason are saved by Christ's merit alone; adults also need their own merit.
Actual faith directs meritorious acts as prudence directs virtuous ones.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1265.summary: Second conclusion: the infused faith in us and in the Old Testament fathers was the same, but not the acquired faith or the act of faith. First part: infused faith is one in each person and the same in species in all, with one immediate principal object (d. 23 q. 2, concl. 6), so it was the same in species, not in number, in them and in us, since numerically one accident cannot be in different subjects under God's ordained power. It does not vary with its mediate or less principal objects, so even if the particular articles differed, the habit remains the same, with the same immediate object, 'everything revealed by God is true', through whose act it inclines to all special articles.
claims: Infused faith was the same in species in the fathers and in us.
Infused faith does not vary with changes in its mediate objects, the particular articles.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1333.summary: Second part, regarding acquired faith in the Redeemer. For some articles (creation, the fall, the future judgment), acquired faith and its act were the same in species for them and for us, so the conclusion holds only particularly. Assent to specifically distinct (non-synonymous) propositions consists of specifically distinct acts, and distinct acts give distinct habits. The fathers believed 'Christ will come, will suffer, will rise', and we believe 'Christ came, suffered, rose'. These are non-synonymous because of different time connotation and are not true together, since when one is true the other is false. A proposition of one species cannot be true and false at once.
claims: Acquired faith about the Redeemer differs in species between the fathers and us.
Future-tense and past-tense propositions about Christ are non-synonymous because of their time connotation.
For some articles, such as creation and judgment, acquired faith is the same for both.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1410.summary: Objection: 'Christ will suffer' and 'Christ has suffered' are the same article, since they express the same matter, Christ's passion, though with different tenses, so the faith is the same.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1428.summary: Reply by distinguishing 'article'. If an article is a revealed truth (as defined at the end of the previous question), the antecedent is denied. The same passion is believed, future for them and past for us, but there can be as many articles about one matter as there are true non-synonymous propositions, and differences in secondary signification such as tense make propositions non-synonymous. If 'article' means the matter about which various propositions are formed, the two are one article, but the inference to the same faith fails, because acquired faith and its acts are distinguished by their immediate objects (the propositional truths), not by the remote object (the signified matter). The objection rests on an equivocation in 'article'.
claims: As revealed truths, 'Christ will suffer' and 'Christ suffered' are distinct articles.
There can be as many articles about one matter as there are non-synonymous true propositions.
Acquired faith is distinguished by its immediate propositional objects, not by its remote object.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1511.summary: Third conclusion: at every time after the fall, explicit faith in the mediator was necessary for salvation for those using reason. No one is saved unless a member of the Church, and so of Christ, and no one is a member except through faith in the mediator (Hebrews 11). As those after Christ's coming, so those before were members of Christ and the Church through the same faith.
claims: Explicit faith in the mediator has been necessary for salvation since the fall.
Membership in the Church and in Christ comes only through faith in the mediator.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1542.summary: Further: as the Creator is the principle of being for created nature, the Redeemer is the principle of restoration for fallen nature. No one can be restored without the Redeemer, as nothing can exist without the Creator, so as faith in the Creator was always necessary, so after the fall was faith in the mediator.
claims: The Redeemer is the principle of restoration as the Creator is the principle of being.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1562.summary: Qualification: faith in the mediator can be particular, that the Son of God would become incarnate and, God and man, redeem the human race by virgin birth and death on the cross. Believing this explicitly was not necessary in every state. It could also be believed more confusedly and generally: that God would ordain some way of redemption through some mediator, without knowing whom (the Word, an angel, or another). This general belief was necessary for everyone after the fall. Those to whom more was revealed were bound to believe more particularly. Under the Mosaic law, with the Redeemer more distinctly revealed in the Law, Prophets, and Psalms, more particular belief was required than under the law of nature, and under the Gospel still more, varying by state of life. So, as Bonaventure says (q. 2 of this distinction), the philosophers, lacking even this general faith and relying on their virtues and merits, could not be members of Christ or be saved.
claims: General faith in some divinely ordained mediator was necessary for all after the fall.
Explicit particular faith in the incarnation was not required in every state.
The required explicitness grows from the law of nature to the Mosaic law to the Gospel, according to revelation received.
The philosophers, lacking even general faith in a mediator, could not be saved.
concepts: general and particular faith in the mediator
law of nature, Mosaic law, Gospel

gbs333-h59932-d1e1634.summary: To the objection that philosophers could not reach this actual faith by their own discovery or teaching: God's grace was available to all, nature itself, by its crookedness and weakness, led them to seek a redeemer, and they could learn from those renowned for worshipping God. So none was excused from at least general faith, and had they done what was in them, God would not have failed to enlighten them. Romans 1: knowing God, they did not glorify him but became vain in their thoughts. They did not act on their natural knowledge by glorifying and diligently seeking God, but diligently sought vain things instead.
claims: No one was excused from general faith in a mediator, since grace, nature's weakness, and available teaching pointed to it.
If the philosophers had done what was in them, God would have enlightened them.
The philosophers failed to act on their natural knowledge of God (Romans 1).

gbs333-h59932-d1e1700.summary: The same applies to someone born in the forest who never heard a teacher of the faith.
claims: The one born in the forest is in the same situation: God provides if he does what is in him.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1707.summary: Cites Aquinas (III Sent. d. 25 q. 2): in what is necessary for salvation God never fails, or failed, one seeking salvation except through that person's fault. The explicit knowledge of what is necessary for salvation is provided by God through a preacher (Cornelius, Acts 10; the Ethiopian eunuch, Acts 8) or by revelation, after which it is in free will's power to make the act of faith.
claims: God never fails one who seeks salvation, except through that person's fault.
God provides necessary explicit knowledge through a preacher or through revelation.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1736.summary: Fourth conclusion: under the Gospel law, all members of the Church are bound to believe the same things, implicitly though not explicitly. The 'not explicitly' part is shown below. That all must believe implicitly follows because all are bound to have infused faith (first conclusion), which implicitly believes everything, being a habit inclining mediately or immediately to all credibles.
claims: All members of the Church are bound to believe the same things implicitly, but not all explicitly.
Infused faith, which all must have, implies implicit belief in all credibles.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1762.summary: Further: everyone with the use of reason is bound to believe that everything revealed by God is true and that Scripture is revealed and true, and one who believes this explicitly implicitly believes all credibles, since all are revealed and contained mediately or immediately in Scripture (cf. Panormitanus on De summa trinitate).
claims: All rational persons must explicitly believe that all revelation and Scripture are true, which is implicit belief in all credibles.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1798.summary: Fifth conclusion: the greater in the Church are bound to believe certain things particularly that the lesser are not. Whoever holds an office in the Church must know as much as the office requires for its lawful and sufficient exercise. Since the greater have the office of teaching, which cannot be done without particular expression of the articles, they must believe distinctly everything they are to explain to the lesser.
claims: Those with teaching office must explicitly and distinctly believe what they must explain to others.
Each office-holder must know what is needed to fulfill the office.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1819.summary: Following Aquinas (III Sent. d. 25 q. 3 a. 3), explication of the articles is twofold: as to the substance of the articles, knowing them distinctly, and as to what is implicitly contained in them, that is, what can be inferred from them and how they are defended against attack.
claims: Explicating the articles concerns either their substance or what they implicitly contain and how they are defended.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1841.summary: All with the office of teaching the faith, whether by rank (priests), revelation (prophets), or ministry (doctors and preachers), are bound to the first, total explication of the substance of the articles, each as far as the office requires.
claims: Priests, prophets, doctors, and preachers must explicitly know the substance of the articles as their office requires.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1862.summary: No one in this life is bound to the second explication perfectly and totally, which is possible only in the homeland. But each one charged with teaching must know as much of it as the office requires, enough for the saving instruction of those entrusted to him, according to their capacity.
claims: Complete explication of what the articles contain is possible only in the homeland.
Teachers must know as much as suffices for the saving instruction of their charges.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1886.summary: Second part: the simple, who have no office of teaching or other ministry, have only to govern themselves, so it suffices for them to believe explicitly those articles by which they can direct their intention to the ultimate end.
claims: The simple need explicitly believe only the articles needed to direct their intention to the last end.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1902.summary: Further, following Scotus: God obliges no one to the impossible, so the lesser and unlearned who cannot grasp certain articles are not bound to believe them explicitly, since nothing can be believed explicitly unless apprehended. Someone so unlearned as not to conceive what a person or a nature is need not have an explicit act about the unity of nature and Trinity of persons distinctly, as literate clerics do. A rough faith suffices for them, that Christ was born and suffered and the like concerning the work of redemption. They are bound to some explicit acts at some time and to others in general, believing as the Church believes.
claims: God does not oblige anyone to the impossible.
Nothing can be believed explicitly unless apprehended.
The very simple need explicit faith only in the work of redemption and implicit faith in the rest, as the Church believes.

gbs333-h59932-d1e1954.summary: Specifies what the lesser must believe explicitly: three things in general, that God exists, that he rewards, and that there is a mediator or redeemer of the human race. The first two come from Hebrews 11, the third from Acts 4 ('there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved'). Augustine (to Optatus): sound faith holds that no one, young or old, is freed from the contagion of death and original sin except by the one mediator Jesus Christ, and the just before his coming were saved by believing he would come in the flesh, so since Adam's fall that name has availed for salvation (cf. third conclusion).
claims: The simple must explicitly believe that God exists, that he rewards, and that there is a redeemer.
No one is freed from original sin except through the one mediator Christ, before or after the incarnation.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2024.summary: The article of the incarnation presupposes the article of the Trinity (Aquinas, II-II q. 2 a. 8): the mystery of Christ cannot be believed explicitly without faith in the Trinity, since it includes that the Son of God took flesh and was conceived by the grace of the Holy Spirit. So after the time of grace was published all must believe the Trinity explicitly, as all reborn in Christ are reborn by invoking the Trinity. Biel interprets this as requiring belief, confusedly or generally, that in the deity there are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and these three are one God, not distinct understanding of personal distinction in unity.
claims: Explicit faith in the incarnation presupposes faith in the Trinity.
Since the Gospel all must explicitly believe the Trinity, but only in a general or confused way.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2072.summary: Faith in the incarnation includes many things about Christ (conception by the Spirit, virgin birth, passion), which is why the apostles ordered the Creed around what principally orders us to salvation, as principles of faith all must believe. Under the Gospel, the Church has ordered feasts through the year celebrating these articles, so no one can excuse ignorance of them. Bonaventure: one must believe explicitly the articles made manifest not only by preaching but by the Church's usage, the Trinity by the sign of the cross 'in the name of the Father...', and the nativity, passion, and resurrection by their solemnities, while other articles may be believed implicitly as the Church believes them. Aquinas (III Sent. d. 25): explicit faith is needed to direct intention to the ultimate end, and since sin turned man from it and only the mediator restores him, after sin explicit knowledge of the Redeemer is needed, especially of how he led us back by conquering the enemy.
claims: The Creed contains the principles of faith that all must believe.
No one can excuse ignorance of articles celebrated in the Church's feasts and usage.
Explicit knowledge of the Redeemer is needed after sin to direct one's intention to the last end.
concepts: faith directing to the last end

gbs333-h59932-d1e2160.summary: Four things were required for Christ to lead us back to the end: that our champion be instituted (nativity), fight (passion), conquer (resurrection, opening eternity by defeating death), and make all his own sharers in his victory (judgment, rendering good to the good and evil to the evil). These especially must be believed explicitly. Since they are expressly in the Creed, all are bound at some time to an act of faith in the Creed's articles. If some are too dull to recite them in order, it suffices that they explicitly believe each when proposed. So all in the time of grace are obliged to explicit faith in everything in the Creed, as Lombard says.
claims: Christ's nativity, passion, resurrection, and judgment must especially be believed explicitly.
All under the Gospel are bound to explicit faith in all the Creed's articles.
The dull need not recite the Creed in order but must believe each article explicitly when proposed.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2215.summary: Beyond this, everyone must explicitly believe any particular truth virtually included in what he believes generally, once it has been sufficiently shown to be so included. For instance, one who believes everything revealed by God is true must explicitly believe any particular revealed truth once it is sufficiently shown to be revealed.
claims: Once a particular truth is sufficiently shown to be contained in one's general faith, one must believe it explicitly.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2237.summary: Sixth conclusion: though the simple and lesser are not bound to explicit faith in each particular credible, all are bound to avoid adhering pertinaciously to any particular error. Every believer must avoid whatever would make him a heretic, and any pertinacious error against a credible in the biblical canon makes one a heretic and removes infused faith, which is necessary for salvation.
claims: All are bound to avoid pertinacious adherence to any error against a scriptural credible.
Any pertinacious error against Scripture makes one a heretic and destroys infused faith.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2281.summary: Objection: no one is bound to avoid an error unless bound to believe its opposite explicitly, and no one is bound to know all errors, which are infinite. Reply: avoiding error is twofold, not consenting to it at all, or not adhering to it pertinaciously. One is not bound to avoid every error in the first way, but in the second, and this requires no knowledge of the error. Whoever has implicit faith in everything in Scripture cannot fall into pertinacious error, being always ready to believe once shown that the error contradicts Scripture. So both the antecedent and its proof are false.
claims: Avoiding error means either not consenting or not adhering pertinaciously; only the latter is universally required.
Implicit faith in Scripture suffices to exclude pertinacious error without knowing the errors.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2340.summary: Seventh and final conclusion, answering the question: all the articles of faith are sufficiently collected in the Apostles' Creed and are specifically distinct from one another. They are sufficient because they virtually and reductively contain all credibles. Every credible in canonical Scripture can be reduced to 'I believe the holy Catholic Church', since to believe this is to believe that the Church holily, truly, and without error approved whatever it approved, including the whole canon with its sacraments, precepts, histories, and everything else. The second part is clear from the first notandum.
claims: The Apostles' Creed sufficiently contains all articles of faith, virtually and reductively.
All scriptural truths are reducible to the article on the holy Catholic Church, which approved the canon.
The articles of the Creed are specifically distinct.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2405.summary: Article 3, first doubt: since the lesser must believe explicitly what is virtually contained in their implicit faith once shown, must they believe a prelate who explicates it particularly? Following Scotus: what is commonly preached in the Church and approved by the usage of feasts (Christ's birth, crucifixion, the Creed's articles) the lesser must believe from their prelates. But if prelates or others preach something not commonly preached elsewhere, newly proposed in one place, the simple are not bound to believe it firmly, and it is better not to adhere until they know the Church holds it. If someone believes it thinking the Church does, even if it is false, he does not sin, provided he does not adhere pertinaciously. Likewise in morals: if someone preaches that a mortal sin is not mortal, it is better not to believe it and to abstain from the act until certified after diligent inquiry, especially if one has heard the opposite preached.
claims: The simple must believe prelates in what is commonly preached and celebrated in the Church.
Novel local teaching need not be firmly believed until known to be the Church's teaching.
Believing an error thinking it the Church's teaching is not sinful if non-pertinacious.
In moral doubt about mortal sin one should abstain until certified.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2480.summary: Second doubt: whether the articles of faith have grown over time. Faith may be said to progress in quantity, in devotion, or in firmness.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2493.summary: In quantity, growth could be by adding new articles or by explicating implicit ones. By addition it has not grown: for every new article added by fulfillment, an old one about future expectation ceased. As 'Christ has come' began to be an article, 'Christ will come' ceased to be one, so the number of articles is unchanged.
claims: The number of articles has not increased, since fulfilled prophecies replace expectations.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2526.summary: In explication, faith has grown, being more clearly explicated with the arrival of the truth than under figurative shadow.
claims: Faith has grown in explicitness since the coming of Christ.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2535.summary: In devotion, faith grew with the fullness of time through the fuller light in showing the truth, the greater diffusion of grace in showing charity, and clearer instruction in preaching the word of salvation. Truth came through Christ, ampler grace is given in the sacraments of the new law through his merit, and the faith is preached more openly ('their sound has gone out into all the earth').
claims: Faith grew in devotion with Christ's coming, through fuller light, more grace in the sacraments, and wider preaching.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2564.summary: In firmness, faith likewise grew, both through greater devotion and clearer knowledge, since faith in articles more openly known and more devoutly embraced is firmer (agreeing with Bonaventure).
claims: Faith is firmer when its articles are more clearly known and more devoutly embraced.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2582.summary: Third doubt: whether the pope or the Church can add a new article to the faith. Answer: in matters of faith, which do not depend on human will, neither pope nor Church can make a false assertion true or a true one false, so neither can they make a non-Catholic truth Catholic or a non-heretical one heretical, nor create or remove an article. Catholic truths are immutably true by the nature of the thing apart from any approval, and so are immutably Catholic, and heresies are false and heretical apart from any condemnation. Proof: taking 'article' and 'truth' as the same, a truth is Catholic either because divinely revealed, contained in Scripture, received by the Church, approved by the pope, or following necessarily from one of these, and there is no other way.
claims: Neither pope nor Church can create or remove an article of faith.
Catholic truths are immutably Catholic apart from any ecclesiastical approval, and heresies are heretical apart from condemnation.
concepts: papal and ecclesial authority over doctrine

gbs333-h59932-d1e2653.summary: If a truth is Catholic because divinely revealed or contained in Scripture, then since revelation depends neither on pope nor Church, their approval contributes nothing to its being Catholic or contained in Scripture.
claims: Revelation and Scripture do not depend on papal or ecclesial approval.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2669.summary: If a truth is Catholic because the Church received it, why did the Church receive it? If because revealed to it or found in Scripture, it is Catholic apart from reception. Not because known by experience or natural reason, since matters of faith exceed these, and otherwise the Church could make geometrical truths articles and false geometrical assertions heresies. If because it pleased the Church, our faith would rest on human will, contrary to 1 Corinthians 2 ('not in persuasive words of human wisdom', still less in human wills).
claims: The Church receives truths as Catholic because they are revealed or scriptural, not by its own will.
Faith cannot rest on natural reason or on human will.
concepts: faith not founded on human will

gbs333-h59932-d1e2734.summary: If a truth is Catholic because it follows from one of the foregoing, it would follow from them even without the Church's approval and reception.
claims: Truths following from revelation are Catholic independently of approval.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2743.summary: If a truth is Catholic because the pope approved it, the same argument as for the Church applies. So no truth is Catholic by the approval of Church or pope. By its approval the Church or pope recognizes and defines that a truth was and is Catholic, and that condemned assertions were and are heretical. It does not make a new article but determines that something belongs and belonged to Catholic truth. Such a truth, though newly defined, does not newly begin to be an article. It was one before, though not known as such by all, and after the definition it is known and held by all. Ockham's Dialogus (I.2.12) treats this at length. So when the Church or pope makes a new creed, as at Nicaea, it does not make new Catholic truths but newly declares that certain truths were and are Catholic. Ockham discusses which truths are to be held Catholic, followed by Gerson and others.
claims: Ecclesial or papal approval recognizes and defines, but does not make, Catholic truth.
A newly defined article was already an article before its definition, though not known by all.
New creeds, such as the Nicene, declare existing Catholic truths rather than creating new ones.

gbs333-h59932-d1e2830.summary: Last doubt: does natural reason brought to show truths of faith diminish the merit of faith, given that some articles are demonstrable (God is living, intelligent; Hebrews 11)? Following Aquinas (II-II q. 2 a. 10), reason can relate to faith in two ways. Antecedently, when someone assents only because a convincing argument compels him and would not otherwise believe, reason diminishes and indeed removes merit, since nothing is meritorious unless voluntary, and such assent is compelled rather than given on divine authority. Consequently, when someone has a ready will to believe on divine authority, loves the believed truth, and seeks reasons, not to believe more firmly (which would put human reason above divine authority) but to understand, defend, and teach it, reason does not remove merit and is a sign of greater merit. Reason does remove acquired faith and its act, since science and acquired faith of the same thing cannot coexist, though science and infused faith can (d. 24, concl. 4). But it does not remove the merit of the will that would believe even without reasons, and it increases merit when charity commands the intellect to seek reasons for God's honor and the gain of souls.
claims: Reason that compels assent, as its sole ground, removes the merit of faith, since merit requires voluntariness.
Reason sought by a believing will to understand, defend, and teach the faith is a sign of greater merit.
Demonstrative reason removes acquired faith of the same truth but not infused faith.
Seeking reasons from charity for God's honor increases merit.

gbs333-h59932.summary: This quaestio unica of III d. 25 asks whether the faithful of both testaments are bound to believe explicitly all the articles of faith distinguished in the Apostles' Creed. Article 1 sets out three notabilia. (1) The Creed, a compendium the apostles composed so all truths could be reduced to it, has fourteen articles by content (seven on the divinity, including creation, justification, and beatification, and seven on Christ's humanity), ordered for ease of understanding and memory. It has twelve by apostolic author, a disputed and unimportant assignment, since the Holy Spirit is its principal author. The Nicene and Athanasian creeds were added against specific heresies. (2) Explicit faith is actual assent to a Catholic truth. Implicit faith is assent to a general proposition (e.g. whatever the Church believes is true) that includes its consequences. One can implicitly believe what one explicitly denies, and implicit faith in the Church's belief protects from heresy and can even preserve merit in invincible error. (3) The faithful divide into the greater, who must teach and defend, and the lesser. Article 2 gives seven conclusions. (1) Infused faith was necessary for salvation in every state of the Church, and actual faith for adults, as charioteer of merit. (2) Infused faith is the same in species in the fathers and in us, but acquired faith in the Redeemer differs, since 'he will come' and 'he came' are non-synonymous. (3) Faith in a mediator has been necessary since the fall, generally for all and more particularly as revelation increased. Philosophers and those raised in the forest are not excused, since God aids whoever does what is in him. (4) All are bound to believe the same things implicitly but not explicitly. (5) The greater must know what their teaching office requires. The simple need explicit faith in God, his rewarding, and the Redeemer, together with the Trinity in a general way and the Creed's articles shown in the Church's feasts. (6) All must avoid pertinacious error, which implicit faith suffices to exclude. (7) The Creed sufficiently contains all articles, since all Scripture reduces to the article on the Church. Article 3 resolves doubts. The simple must believe what is commonly preached, not local novelties. The articles have not grown in number but in explication, devotion, and firmness. Neither pope nor Church can create an article, only define and declare existing Catholic truth (Ockham). Reason removes merit when it compels assent but increases it when sought by charity to understand and defend the faith.
claims: The Apostles' Creed sufficiently contains all articles of faith, since all Scripture reduces to the article on the Church.
Implicit faith in whatever the Church believes protects against heresy and can preserve merit despite invincible error.
Infused faith, and actual faith for adults, was necessary for salvation in every state of the Church.
Infused faith is the same in both testaments, but acquired faith in the Redeemer differs with the tense of its propositions.
General faith in a mediator has been necessary for salvation since the fall, with the required explicitness growing with revelation.
All must believe the same things implicitly, but explicit faith is required according to office and capacity.
The simple must explicitly believe that God exists and rewards, that Christ is Redeemer, the Trinity in a general way, and the articles celebrated by the Church.
All must avoid pertinacious adherence to error, which implicit faith suffices to prevent.
The articles have not increased in number but have grown in explication, devotion, and firmness.
Neither pope nor Church can make new articles; they only define what was always Catholic truth.
Reason as the sole ground of assent removes merit, but reason sought by a believing will increases it.
concepts: ecclesial and papal authority over doctrine
